scope: New canonical references for the demographic explanation cards and same-person intention/outcome chart. Imported demographic and reproductive evidence; no source identifies the BERM L2 bridge.

references.authors: Lutz W, Skirbekk V, Testa MR
references.title: The Low-Fertility Trap Hypothesis: Forces that May Lead to Further Postponement and Fewer Births in Europe
references.finding: Proposes three reinforcing demographic, ideal-family-size and relative-income mechanisms. Fewer potential mothers reduce future birth numbers; intergenerational norm formation and rising aspirations relative to expected income may reinforce low fertility. The authors expressly decline to establish a universal TFR 1.5 threshold.
references.verification: Publisher full PDF retrieved and checked, including abstract and discussion of McDonald's threshold. The original has three authors, including Maria Rita Testa; it is a hypothesis paper, not a measured infant-contact or endocrine intervention.

references.title: The Unfolding Story of the Second Demographic Transition
references.finding: Develops the SDT account of changing values, household formation and parenthood timing in Europe and industrialized Asia. Explicitly explains a positive contemporary SDT–TFR association through different postponement and subsequent recuperation patterns, rather than a uniform negative cultural coefficient.
references.verification: Publisher metadata and author abstract checked; author-deposited January 2010 working text also consulted. This is a theoretical and demographic synthesis, not a physiological measurement of preferences.

references.authors: Mahler L, Tertilt M, Yum M
references.title: Policy Concerns in an Era of Low Fertility: The Role of Social Comparisons and Intensive Parenting
references.finding: A formal model shows social comparison can raise parental time and money investments and amplify fertility declines driven by other forces. Cross-country and US regional proxy associations provide suggestive support; the paper explicitly leaves causal identification outside its scope.
references.verification: Final publisher PDF, posted June 2026 for Fall 2025 volume, checked at pages 293–296 and 301. Main article pagination is 293–346; the downloadable file also contains commentary. Figure 5 ideal-family-size versus period-TFR comparison is not used as a within-person intention gap.

references.title: The Correspondence Between Fertility Intentions and Behavior in the United States
references.finding: US NLSY79 participants' expected total family size at about age 24 was compared with their own number of children in 2006, ages 41–50. Table 2 reports fewer, equal or more children than expected for 34.9%, 43.4%, 21.7% of women and 42.8%, 34.2%, 23.0% of men, respectively.
references.verification: Full primary manuscript and Table 2 checked. Women n=3783, men n=3584; all analyses use 2006 sampling weights. The outcome does not establish completed male reproduction. The study does not measure field exposure or directly measure fecundity.

references.title: On the Quantum and Tempo of Fertility
references.finding: Separates fertility quantum from timing effects: postponement can depress period TFR independently of a corresponding decline in lifetime births. Proposes a parity-specific tempo adjustment under stated schedule assumptions; this adjusted estimate is not itself observed completed cohort fertility.
references.verification: Primary Population Council repository abstract and metadata checked. Repository hosts the corresponding working paper; its 10.31899/pgy6.1010 identifier is distinct from the journal article DOI used here.

references.title: Can assisted reproduction technology compensate for the natural decline in fertility with age? A model assessment
references.finding: A reproductive simulation combining age-specific conception, miscarriage and permanent sterility with two IVF cycles estimated partial compensation for delayed childbearing. It recovered about half of births lost by delaying attempts from age 30 to 35 and less than 30% of those lost from 35 to 40 under its treatment assumptions.
references.verification: Primary article abstract checked. These are model outputs using treatment success assumptions available in 2004, not observed contemporary success rates or an individual prognosis.

references.authors: Smith ADAC, Tilling K, Nelson SM, Lawlor DA
references.title: Live-Birth Rate Associated With Repeat In Vitro Fertilization Treatment Cycles
references.finding: UK registry follow-up of 156947 women starting IVF in 2003–2010 found 29.5% live births in the first stimulation cycle including resulting fresh/frozen transfers. With own oocytes, first-cycle rates were 32.3% below age 40 and 12.3% at 40–42. Repeat-cycle cumulative estimates depended on assumptions about treatment discontinuation.
references.verification: Primary abstract and Table 2 checked. Follow-up through June 2012. The six-cycle 65.3% estimate is prognosis-adjusted, not a directly observed fraction of all entrants. Donor-oocyte results lacked the same age gradient; bypass results do not identify the initial environmental etiology.

morgan_rackin_table_2_panel_a.baseline_measure: Expected total family size: existing children plus expected additional children
morgan_rackin_table_2_panel_a.outcome_measure: Same person's reported number of children
morgan_rackin_table_2_panel_a.unit: Percent of respondents in the sex-specific analytic sample
morgan_rackin_table_2_panel_a.display: Two horizontal 100% stacked bars; visible category labels and values; no period TFR or population ideals
morgan_rackin_table_2_panel_a.scope: A within-person discrepancy; not a measured diagnosis of reproductive impairment or its origin
